cs-basics.md:
## Why it exists
You can build apps without knowing how a computer works, until something is slow, leaks memory, deadlocks, or returns `0.30000000000000004`. These ideas are the vocabulary behind every later lesson: why Node's event loop matters, why containers are lighter than virtual machines, why an index makes a query fast, why a serverless cold start hurts.

{{dg:0}}

Mental model: a computer is a very fast worker (CPU) with a tiny desk (registers and caches), a big shelf nearby (RAM) and a warehouse far away (disk and network). Programs are fast when the data they need is already on the desk.

## How it works
- **CPU, RAM, storage.** The CPU executes instructions. RAM is fast and temporary. SSD and disk are slower and persistent. The network is slower again. Approximate latencies: CPU cache around 1 ns, RAM around 100 ns, SSD around 100 microseconds, a round trip inside a datacenter around 0.5 ms, across continents 100 ms or more. The gaps are orders of magnitude, which is why caching exists.
- **Process.** A running program with its own isolated memory. The OS schedules processes; one cannot read another's memory. Docker containers are processes with extra isolation (namespaces, cgroups), not tiny VMs.
- **Thread.** A unit of execution inside a process. Threads share the process memory, which makes sharing cheap and races possible. A **context switch** (the OS pausing one thread and running another) has a cost, so thousands of threads is not free.
- **Stack and heap.** The **call stack** stores function calls and local variables; each call pushes a frame and returning pops it. Too deep (infinite recursion) causes a stack overflow. The **heap** stores objects that outlive a single call; languages with garbage collection (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java) reclaim unreachable objects automatically, and a **memory leak** is memory you still reference but no longer need.
- **Virtual memory.** Each process sees its own large address space; the OS and CPU map it to physical RAM or swap. Running out of RAM causes swapping (very slow) or the OOM killer, which is why containers get memory limits.
- **Compiled vs interpreted.** Compiled languages (Go, Rust, C) translate to machine code ahead of time. Interpreted and JIT-compiled languages (Python, JavaScript on V8) translate while running. This affects startup time, speed and how errors appear.
- **Concurrency vs parallelism.** Concurrency is handling many tasks that overlap in time (an event loop serving 10,000 sockets). Parallelism is executing at the same instant on several cores. I/O-bound work benefits from concurrency (async); CPU-bound work needs parallelism (processes, worker threads).
- **Big-O notation** describes how work grows with input size n: O(1) constant, O(log n) binary search, O(n) one pass, O(n log n) good sorting, O(n^2) nested loops. It ignores constants, so measure too.
- **Numbers and text.** Computers store binary. Decimal fractions like 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in floating point (IEEE 754), so never use floats for money; use integers of cents or a decimal type. Text is bytes plus an encoding; **UTF-8** is the web default and one character can be 1 to 4 bytes.

## Worked example
Four classic surprises, runnable in Python:

```python
import sys, timeit

# 1. Floating point
print(0.1 + 0.2)                  # 0.30000000000000004
from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))   # 0.3  (use for money, or store cents as int)

# 2. Characters are not bytes
s = "café"
print(len(s), len(s.encode("utf-8")))    # 4 characters, 5 bytes

# 3. The call stack has a limit
print(sys.getrecursionlimit())           # 1000 by default
def down(n): return down(n + 1)
try:
    down(0)
except RecursionError as e:
    print("stack exhausted:", type(e).__name__)

# 4. Same question, different data structure
data = list(range(1_000_000))
as_set = set(data)
print("list:", timeit.timeit(lambda: 999_999 in data, number=100))   # O(n) scan
print("set: ", timeit.timeit(lambda: 999_999 in as_set, number=100)) # O(1) hash lookup
```

You will see the set lookup run thousands of times faster. That single choice is the difference between a page that loads and a request that times out.

## In real products
- **Cold starts and memory limits.** Serverless functions start a new process; bigger dependencies mean slower startup, and exceeding the memory limit kills the process.
- **Connection pools.** Each database connection costs memory and a process or thread on the server, so apps share a small pool (see the Postgres lessons).
- **Node and Python async.** One thread plus an event loop handles many sockets; a CPU-heavy loop blocks everything.
- **Observability.** CPU, memory, GC pauses and p99 latency map directly to the concepts above.
- **Money, IDs and time.** Integer cents for money, UUIDs or 64-bit integers for IDs (JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53), UTC timestamps stored as `timestamptz`.

## Trade-offs
| Choice | Gain | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Threads | Simple model, shared memory, real parallelism in many languages | Races, deadlocks, per-thread memory |
| Processes | Isolation, crash containment | Slower to start, harder to share data |
| Async / event loop | Massive I/O concurrency on one thread | Blocking code stalls everything; harder stack traces |
| Cache in RAM | Orders of magnitude faster reads | Staleness, memory pressure, invalidation bugs |
| Compiled language | Speed, small deployable binary | Slower iteration loop |

> [!pitfall] Using floats for currency or comparing floats with `==`. Compare with a tolerance or use integers.
> [!pitfall] Assuming O(n) is fine because it was fast with 100 rows. Test with realistic sizes; a nested loop over 100,000 rows is 10 billion steps.
> [!pitfall] Reading a whole file or API response into memory. Stream it instead (see the Node streams lesson).
> [!tip] Measure before optimizing: profilers and `timeit` beat intuition, and most slowness is one hot spot or one N+1 query.
> [!prod] When a service is "randomly slow", check in this order: CPU saturation, memory and GC, thread or connection pool exhaustion, slow dependency, then network.
q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
A process is an isolated program instance with its own memory; threads are execution paths inside a process that share that memory. Sharing is cheap but causes races.
Why does `0.1 + 0.2` not equal `0.3` and what should you use for money?
Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. Use a decimal type or integer cents.
When does concurrency help, and when do you need parallelism?
Concurrency (async) helps I/O-bound work where tasks wait on networks or disks; CPU-bound work needs parallel execution on multiple cores via processes or worker threads.
What happens on a stack overflow and what causes it?
The call stack runs out of space, usually from unbounded recursion; the runtime raises an error or crashes. Convert to a loop or bound the depth.
Why is `x in some_set` faster than `x in some_list` for large collections?
A set uses a hash table with O(1) average lookup; a list scans elements, O(n).

cs-how-computers-work.md:
## Why it exists

Software abstractions leak. Sooner or later a bug or a bottleneck is explained by something below the language: a number that wrapped around, a decimal that is off by a hair, a name with an accent that sorts or counts wrong, a loop that is ten times faster when it walks memory in a different order, a service whose latency is dominated by cache misses. Engineers who understand **how data is represented** and **how the machine moves it** diagnose these in minutes, because the strange behavior is not strange at all, just the hardware and encodings doing exactly what they were designed to do.

**Mental model:** a computer is a device that moves and transforms **bits** very fast, through a **hierarchy of memories** that trade size for speed. Everything you handle (numbers, text, images, programs) is a pattern of bits plus a convention for interpreting it. And nearly all performance comes down to one fact: the CPU is extremely fast and memory is comparatively slow, so the hardware bets heavily on **locality** (you will reuse what you just touched, and touch what is next to it). Respect those two ideas, **representation conventions** and **locality**, and a great deal of "mysterious" behavior becomes predictable.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

### Bits, bytes and number bases

A **bit** is 0 or 1; a **byte** is 8 bits (values 0 to 255, or two hexadecimal digits). Humans use **hexadecimal** (base 16: 0 to 9 then a to f) because each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two digits (`0xFF` is 255). Bitwise operations work directly on bits: AND (`&`) masks, OR (`|`) sets, XOR (`^`) toggles, NOT (`~`) inverts, and shifts (`<<`, `>>`) multiply or divide by powers of two. They appear in permissions flags, network masks (`192.168.1.0/24` means the first 24 bits are the network), hashing, compression and protocols. `n & (n - 1) == 0` tests for a power of two.

### Integers: fixed width, two's complement and overflow

Hardware stores integers in a fixed number of bits. **Unsigned** integers of width w hold 0 to 2^w - 1. **Signed** integers use **two's complement**: the top bit has negative weight, so an 8-bit signed byte holds -128 to 127, and the bit pattern `11111111` is -1. Arithmetic wraps on overflow: in C, Java, Go and Rust (release mode), `127 + 1` in an 8-bit signed type becomes -128; a 32-bit signed integer overflows past 2,147,483,647 (the famous "Year 2038" problem for 32-bit Unix timestamps). Real bugs from this include financial sums, array index calculations and security vulnerabilities (integer overflow leading to a too-small allocation, then a buffer overflow). **Python integers are arbitrary precision** (no overflow, but slower), while JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats, so integers above 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991) lose precision, which is why large ids should be strings or `BigInt`. **Endianness** is byte order: little-endian machines (x86, most ARM) store the least significant byte first; network protocols use big-endian ("network byte order"), so binary formats must convert.

### Floating point: approximate by design

Decimals are stored as **IEEE 754** binary floating point: a sign, an exponent and a fraction (a 64-bit double has 53 bits of precision, about 15 to 17 decimal digits). Many decimal fractions such as 0.1 have no exact binary form, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Consequences: never compare floats for exact equality (use a tolerance), never use floats for money (use integer minor units or a decimal type), expect rounding error to accumulate in long sums (use `math.fsum` or Kahan summation), and know the special values (`NaN`, which is not equal to itself, and positive and negative infinity). Floats also lose precision when numbers differ hugely in size: `1e16 + 1 == 1e16`. Machine learning deliberately uses smaller formats (float16, bfloat16, int8) to trade precision for speed and memory (see the deep learning lesson).

### Text: characters, code points and bytes

Computers store numbers, so text needs an **encoding**. **ASCII** maps 128 characters to 7 bits. **Unicode** assigns every character in every writing system (and emoji) a **code point** (`U+0041` is "A", `U+1F600` is a grinning face), over a million possible. A code point must still be turned into bytes: **UTF-8** (the dominant encoding on the web and in APIs) uses 1 byte for ASCII and 2 to 4 bytes for everything else, is backward compatible with ASCII and has no byte-order problem; **UTF-16** (used by JavaScript and Java strings internally, and Windows) uses 2 or 4 bytes. Key lessons: **bytes and strings are different types**, and you must decode and encode at the edges (files, network, databases) with an explicit encoding (almost always UTF-8); the **length** of text depends on what you count (bytes, UTF-16 units, code points, or user-perceived **grapheme clusters**: `"e\u0301"` renders as one "é" but is two code points; a family emoji can be seven code points); the same visible text can have different code point sequences, so **normalize** (NFC) before comparing or hashing; case conversion and sorting are locale-dependent (the Turkish dotted and dotless i); and mojibake (garbled text like "Ã©") means bytes decoded with the wrong encoding. Never truncate UTF-8 or UTF-16 strings at an arbitrary byte or index without respecting character boundaries.

### Inside the CPU

A CPU repeats the **fetch, decode, execute** cycle on **machine instructions** (add, load, store, compare, jump), holding working values in a few dozen **registers**. Modern cores run billions of instructions per second by overlapping work: **pipelining** (several instructions in flight at once), **superscalar** execution (several per cycle), **out-of-order** execution (reordering independent instructions) and **branch prediction** (guessing which way an `if` will go so the pipeline stays full; a wrong guess costs on the order of 10 to 20 cycles). **SIMD** instructions apply one operation to many values at once (the basis of fast numeric libraries and part of why NumPy loops outrun Python loops), and **multiple cores** run threads in parallel, which brings synchronization and cache-coherence costs. Clock speeds stopped rising quickly around the mid-2000s, so performance gains since then come from more cores, wider vectors, better caches and specialization (GPUs, TPUs and other accelerators).

### The memory hierarchy and locality

Fast memory is small and expensive; big memory is slow. Approximate, order-of-magnitude access times (they have changed little in shape for years):

| Level | Typical size | Latency |
|---|---|---|
| Register | tens of values | under 1 ns |
| L1 cache | tens of KB per core | about 1 ns |
| L2 cache | hundreds of KB to a few MB | about 3 to 5 ns |
| L3 cache | tens of MB, shared | about 10 to 40 ns |
| Main memory (RAM) | GBs | about 60 to 100 ns |
| NVMe SSD | hundreds of GB to TB | about 20 to 100 microseconds |
| Spinning disk | TBs | about 5 to 10 ms |
| Network, same data center | n/a | about 0.5 ms |
| Network, across continents | n/a | about 100 to 200 ms |

A RAM access costs on the order of a hundred times an L1 hit, so the cache's job is vital. Memory moves in **cache lines** (commonly 64 bytes): touching one byte brings its neighbors along for free. This rewards **spatial locality** (use data stored next to each other: arrays and contiguous structures beat pointer-chasing linked lists and trees of small objects) and **temporal locality** (reuse recent data). It explains why iterating a 2D array in the memory's own order (row by row in C and NumPy's default layout) can be several times faster than the transposed order, why arrays of structs versus structs of arrays matters for hot loops, why Python lists of objects are slow compared with NumPy arrays (pointers to scattered objects versus a packed buffer), and why databases and columnar formats store related data contiguously. **Virtual memory, paging and the page cache** add another layer (see the OS concepts lesson), and **false sharing** (two threads writing different variables on the same cache line) can quietly destroy multi-core scaling.

### From source code to running program

Source code becomes execution in several ways. A **compiler** translates the whole program ahead of time into machine code for a specific CPU (C, C++, Rust, Go): fast to run, a build step to ship. An **interpreter** reads and executes the program step by step (classic Python, Ruby, shell): flexible and portable, slower. Most "interpreted" languages actually compile to **bytecode** first (Python's `dis` module shows it) and run it on a **virtual machine**. A **JIT (just-in-time) compiler** watches which code is hot and compiles it to machine code at run time (the JVM, .NET, V8 for JavaScript, PyPy), combining portability with high steady-state speed at the cost of warm-up time. The compile pipeline: **lexing** (text into tokens), **parsing** (tokens into a tree, the **AST**), analysis and optimization, then code generation. **Linking** combines compiled pieces and libraries into an executable, and the **loader** maps it into memory when you run it. The **call stack** holds a frame per active function (arguments, local variables, return address); the **heap** holds dynamically allocated objects. Compilers also optimize aggressively (inlining, loop unrolling, vectorization), which is why benchmarking unoptimized code misleads.

### Files, formats and checksums

Files are bytes plus a convention: text formats (JSON, CSV, YAML, source code) are readable with a text editor if you know the encoding; binary formats (images, Parquet, Protobuf, executables) need their specification. A "magic number" at the start often identifies the type (`PK` for ZIP, `%PDF`, `\x89PNG`). `xxd` or `hexdump -C` show the raw bytes. A **hash function** maps data to a fixed-size fingerprint: cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) detect tampering and identify content; non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, MurmurHash) distribute keys quickly for hash tables. A **checksum or CRC** detects accidental corruption. **Compression** exploits redundancy (gzip and zstd for general data, JPEG and AV1 lossy for media). **Encoding binary as text** (Base64 expands data by about a third) lets bytes travel through text-only channels.

## Worked example

Everything below is runnable in plain Python and demonstrates the ideas above.

**1) Two's complement, overflow and bit tricks:**

```python
def to_signed(value: int, bits: int) -> int:
    """Interpret the low `bits` bits of value as a two's complement signed integer."""
    value &= (1 << bits) - 1
    return value - (1 << bits) if value >> (bits - 1) else value

print(to_signed(0b11111111, 8))              # -1
print(to_signed(127 + 1, 8))                 # -128: 8-bit signed overflow wraps around
print(to_signed(2_147_483_647 + 1, 32))      # -2147483648: the 32-bit overflow behind Year 2038
print(bin(0b1011_0110 & 0b0000_1111), hex(0xDEADBEEF >> 16))   # masks and shifts
n = 64
print((n & (n - 1)) == 0)                    # True: 64 is a power of two

print(2**53, float(2**53) + 1 == float(2**53))   # True: doubles cannot count past 2**53 exactly
```

**2) Floating point is approximate, and how to cope:**

```python
import math
from decimal import Decimal

print(0.1 + 0.2, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # 0.30000000000000004 False True
total = 0.0
for _ in range(10):
    total += 0.1
print(total == 1.0, math.fsum([0.1] * 10) == 1.0)               # False True: naive adds drift, fsum tracks lost low bits
print(1e16 + 1 == 1e16)                                              # True: the +1 vanishes
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))             # True: decimal arithmetic for money
nan = float("nan"); print(nan == nan, math.isnan(nan))               # False True
```

**3) Text: code points, bytes, normalization and grapheme surprises:**

```python
import unicodedata

s = "caf\u00e9"                        # "café" with a precomposed é
t = "cafe\u0301"                       # "café" as e plus a combining accent
print(s == t, len(s), len(t))                                  # False 4 5: same look, different code points
print(unicodedata.normalize("NFC", t) == s)                    # True: normalize before comparing
print(s.encode("utf-8"), len(s.encode("utf-8")))               # b'caf\xc3\xa9' 5 bytes
print("\U0001F600".encode("utf-8"), len("\U0001F600".encode("utf-16-le")) // 2)   # 4 bytes in UTF-8, 2 UTF-16 units
family = "\U0001F468\u200D\U0001F469\u200D\U0001F467"           # one family emoji
print(len(family), len(family.encode("utf-8")))                # 5 code points, 18 bytes, but looks like 1 character
print(s.encode("utf-8").decode("latin-1"))                      # 'cafÃ©': mojibake from decoding with the wrong encoding
```

**4) Locality: the same sum, two traversal orders.** Memory layout decides speed even in Python (the effect is far larger in C or NumPy):

```python
import time, array

N = 2000
flat = array.array("d", [1.0]) * (N * N)          # a contiguous N x N matrix stored row by row

def sum_row_major():
    total = 0.0
    for r in range(N):
        base = r * N
        for c in range(N):
            total += flat[base + c]               # walks memory sequentially
    return total

def sum_col_major():
    total = 0.0
    for c in range(N):
        for r in range(N):
            total += flat[r * N + c]              # jumps N*8 bytes each step: many cache misses
    return total

for fn in (sum_row_major, sum_col_major):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(); print(f"{fn.__name__:15s} {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s")
```

On most machines the column-order walk is slower even though it does identical arithmetic (about 40% slower in a test run here, 0.22 s versus 0.31 s); interpreter overhead hides much of the gap, and rewriting it with NumPy or in C shows the cache effect much more starkly. Try changing `N` and watching the gap grow once the matrix no longer fits in cache.

**5) Look at bytes, hashes and bytecode:**

```python
import dis, hashlib, struct

data = struct.pack("<I", 0xDEADBEEF)              # little-endian 32-bit integer
print(data.hex(" "), struct.pack(">I", 0xDEADBEEF).hex(" "))   # ef be ad de vs de ad be ef: endianness

print(hashlib.sha256(b"hello").hexdigest()[:16])  # same input, same fingerprint; any change alters everything
print(hashlib.sha256(b"hellp").hexdigest()[:16])

def add(a, b):
    return a + b
dis.dis(add)                                      # the bytecode the Python VM runs
```

## In real products

- **Databases and file formats** are designed around the memory hierarchy: B-trees pack many keys per page to minimize disk reads, columnar formats (Parquet) store a column contiguously for scans and compression, and LSM trees convert random writes into sequential ones because sequential I/O is far faster than random.
- **Scientific and ML software** relies on contiguous arrays, SIMD and GPUs; libraries such as NumPy, BLAS and PyTorch exist because looping in the interpreter wastes the hardware, and reduced-precision formats (bfloat16, int8, quantization) trade precision for speed.
- **Games and high-frequency trading** structure data for cache locality (arrays of structs, data-oriented design), avoid allocation in hot paths and measure in nanoseconds.
- **Internationalized products** (every global app) handle UTF-8, normalization, collation and grapheme-aware text editing; bugs here show up as corrupted names, broken search and security issues such as homograph spoofing.
- **Financial systems** use decimal or integer minor-unit arithmetic, never binary floats, and audit for overflow; the 2038 timestamp issue and legacy two-digit years have driven large remediation projects.
- **Language runtimes** (V8, the JVM, .NET, PyPy) use JIT compilation and sophisticated garbage collectors, trading warm-up and memory for peak performance, which is why benchmarks must include warm-up and steady-state phases.

> [!pitfall] Using floats for money or exact comparison. Binary floats cannot represent most decimals exactly, so totals drift and equality checks fail. Use integer cents or a decimal type, round at defined points, and compare with a tolerance when floats are unavoidable.
> [!pitfall] Mixing bytes and text or assuming an encoding. Reading a file without specifying UTF-8, or decoding bytes with the wrong codec, yields mojibake or crashes on the first non-ASCII character. Decode and encode explicitly at every boundary, and store and transmit UTF-8.
> [!pitfall] Treating string length as the number of user-visible characters. Truncating by index can cut an emoji or an accent in half, and database column limits count bytes or code points differently. Use grapheme-aware libraries for UI limits and normalize before comparing.
> [!pitfall] Silent integer overflow and precision loss: 32-bit counters, 32-bit timestamps, JavaScript ids above 2^53, and multiplication before a size check. Use wide enough types, check ranges, send large ids as strings, and prefer languages or modes that trap overflow where correctness matters.
> [!pitfall] Guessing at performance. Hardware effects (cache misses, branch mispredictions, allocation, false sharing) are invisible in source code. Profile with realistic data, benchmark with warm-up and several runs, and distrust a micro-benchmark that the compiler may have optimized away.
> [!security] Many classic vulnerabilities come from representation mistakes: integer overflow leading to a small allocation and a buffer overflow, signed and unsigned confusion in length checks, Unicode normalization differences that bypass filters or enable lookalike-domain spoofing, and timing side channels from non-constant-time comparisons. Validate sizes before arithmetic, normalize and canonicalize input before security checks, use memory-safe languages where possible, and use constant-time comparison for secrets.
> [!prod] Make representations explicit in contracts: state the encoding (UTF-8), time format (UTC ISO 8601 or epoch with units), numeric types and ranges, and byte order for binary protocols. Test with awkward data (emoji, combining accents, right-to-left text, very large and negative numbers, leap days) and include them in fixtures.
> [!cost] Data layout is a cost lever: compact representations (integers instead of strings, columnar and compressed formats, smaller numeric types) cut memory, storage and network bills, while cache-friendly access patterns do the same work on fewer, cheaper machines. Measure before and after, since the wrong micro-optimization costs engineering time.
> [!tip] When behavior surprises you, drop one level: print the bytes (`.encode()`, `hexdump`), the bits (`bin()`), the type and width, or the bytecode (`dis`). A thirty-second look at the underlying representation often explains what an hour of staring at the high-level code cannot.
q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in most languages?
Doubles store binary fractions, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so the sum is slightly off (0.30000000000000004). Compare with a tolerance and use integers or decimals for money.
What happens when a signed 8-bit integer holding 127 is incremented in a language without overflow checks?
It wraps to -128 under two's complement. The same wrap-around happens at 2,147,483,647 for 32-bit integers, the cause of the Year 2038 problem for 32-bit timestamps.
Why can two strings that look identical be unequal, and what do you do about it?
They may use different code point sequences (a precomposed e-acute versus e plus a combining accent). Normalize to the same form (NFC) before comparing or hashing.
Why is walking a 2D array in memory order faster than the transposed order?
Memory moves in cache lines, so sequential access reuses data already loaded, while strided access misses the cache on nearly every step. RAM access costs about a hundred times an L1 hit.
What is the difference between a compiler, an interpreter and a JIT?

A compiler translates ahead of time to machine code; an interpreter executes the program step by step; a JIT compiles hot code at run time (the JVM, V8, .NET), combining portability with high steady-state speed.
Why must you specify an encoding when reading text files?
Bytes and text are different types; the same bytes decode differently under different encodings, so a wrong guess yields mojibake or errors. Use UTF-8 explicitly at every boundary.
